history.heading: Origins
paragraphs: The western edge of the Iberian Peninsula was home to Celtic and Lusitanian peoples, who resisted Roman conquest. The region became the Roman province of Lusitania. After the Visigoths, Muslim Moors ruled from 711, leaving a lasting influence on culture and language.

The County of Portugal emerged in the north, and in 1139 Afonso Henriques declared himself king. Portugal's borders were essentially fixed by 1249, making them among the oldest in Europe. The 1386 Treaty of Windsor with England is the oldest alliance still in force.

history.heading: The Age of Discovery
paragraphs: In the 15th century, Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored voyages along the African coast. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498, and Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil in 1500. Portugal built a global empire of trading posts and colonies, from Brazil to Angola, Mozambique, Goa, Macau and Timor, and was a major participant in the Atlantic slave trade.
Lisbon was destroyed by a great earthquake and tsunami in 1755 and rebuilt under the Marquis of Pombal. During Napoleon's invasion, the royal court fled to Brazil, which became independent in 1822.

history.heading: Republic, dictatorship and democracy
paragraphs: The monarchy was overthrown in 1910. Instability led to the Estado Novo dictatorship of António de Oliveira Salazar from 1933, which lasted until 1974 and fought costly colonial wars in Africa.

The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974, a largely bloodless military coup welcomed by the population, restored democracy, and the African colonies became independent. Portugal joined the European Community in 1986 and adopted the euro in 1999. Macau was handed to China in 1999. A debt crisis led to an international bailout in 2011.

culture.heading: Language and traditions
paragraphs: Portuguese is spoken by over 250 million people worldwide. Most Portuguese are Catholic, and Fátima is a major pilgrimage site. Fado, melancholic songs expressing saudade (a deep longing), is recognised by UNESCO. Azulejos, painted tiles, decorate buildings across the country.
Poet Luís de Camões wrote the national epic The Lusiads, and José Saramago won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998. Fernando Pessoa is a major modernist poet.

culture.heading: Food and football
paragraphs: Portuguese cuisine features bacalhau (salt cod, said to have 365 recipes), grilled sardines, pastéis de nata (custard tarts) and port wine from the Douro Valley. Football is a passion; Cristiano Ronaldo is a national icon, and Portugal won the European Championship in 2016.

politics.heading: Semi-presidential republic
paragraphs: Portugal is a semi-presidential republic. The directly elected president can dissolve parliament and veto laws, while the prime minister leads the government. The centre-left Socialist Party and centre-right Social Democratic Party have dominated, while the right-wing Chega party has grown rapidly, becoming the second-largest party in 2025. Frequent snap elections have taken place since 2022.
Portugal is a founding member of NATO and a member of the EU and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Portugal's economy relies on services, especially tourism, which has boomed, as well as manufacturing (cars, textiles, footwear, cork, of which Portugal is the world's largest producer, and paper), wine and renewable energy, which supplies most of its electricity.

Since the debt crisis, Portugal has reduced its public debt and attracted tech companies and foreign residents. High housing costs, low wages compared with the EU average and emigration of young people are challenges. The currency is the euro.
